metadata.title: Two Agents Read a Patent — Claims and Lineage with Claude
metadata.note: Mycroft patent intelligence system. Real build history: ODP→PatentsView→BigQuery data-source pivot (Week 6), BigQuery schema verified by hand (Week 7). NotImplementedError design choice in claims_agent.py/lineage_agent.py is real, not illustrative.

beats.role_note: COLD OPEN LAW — Claude UI, ask shown answered
beats.narration_text: A patent abstract is marketing language. The claims section is the legal artifact. Design two agents that read the second one, not the first.

props.command: claude "design a two-agent system: one reads a patent's claims section for legal scope, one traces its citation network for research lineage"
output: Claims Agent: reads independent + dependent claims, classifies protection scope
Lineage Agent: backward citations (what it builds on), forward (what cites it)
Coordinator: flags disagreement between the two readings — does not resolve it silently

beats.narration_text: Method: the claims section is a numbered list of legal statements defining what a patent actually protects — broad and offensive, or narrow and defensive. Most patent analysis tools never read it; they read the abstract, which is plain-English marketing copy, or they just count filings per quarter. Use this when you need to know what a company's patents actually cover, not how many they filed. Where it fails: claims are written to be ambiguous on purpose — a model trained to summarize technical text will often produce a clean technical summary that loses the legal subtext entirely. That gap is the whole reason this needs two agents instead of one prompt.
beats.visual_intent: Split screen: left shows a patent abstract (plain paragraph, highlighted 'marketing language'), right shows a numbered claims list (highlighted 'the legal artifact'); arrow labeled 'most tools only read this side' pointing at the abstract

beats.role_note: ClaudeComposerAsk — show and discuss the prompt
beats.narration_text: Into Claude Code. Scaffold a Claims Agent that pulls full patent text from USPTO's data source, extracts the claims section specifically, and produces a structured reading: what the independent claim protects, how dependent claims narrow it, a defensive-offensive-exploratory classification, and — required — an explicit statement of what the reading is not confident about.

props.command: claude "scaffold a ClaimsAgent class: read_claims(patent_number) -> structured reading of independent + dependent claims, protection-scope classification, and an explicit confidence caveat. Do not implement the USPTO call until a real API key and one real response exist."

beats.role_note: ClaudeCodeBeat — real claims_agent.py excerpt, trimmed to the lines that teach
beats.narration_text: Read the method that matters. It does not parse a guessed API response. It raises NotImplementedError, on purpose, with a reason attached. Writing parsing logic against a schema you have never actually seen produces code that looks finished and is quietly wrong the first time it hits a real response. An honest stop is worth more than a confident guess.

props.title: claims_agent.py
props.code:
class ClaimsAgent:
    def read_claims(self, patent_number: str, claims_text: str) -> ClaimsReading:
        """
        NOT YET IMPLEMENTED. Blocked on having real claims text to
        test the prompt against — running this against placeholder
        text would validate nothing real and risks the prompt
        looking 'done' when it hasn't been checked against an
        actual patent's ambiguous legal language.
        """
        raise NotImplementedError(
            "Waiting on real claims text from USPTOClient before "
            "this is implemented and tested."
        )
props.sparkLine: An honest stop beats a guess.

beats.role_note: animated slot — the honest blocked state, not a fabricated result
beats.narration_text: Run it. Nothing crashes, and nothing pretends to work either. The client raises a clear error naming exactly what's missing: a real USPTO Open Data Portal key, and one inspected response to build the parser against. That's the correct output for this state — not a silent failure, not a plausible-looking fake result.
beats.visual_intent: Terminal-style animation: command runs, error message types out clearly naming the missing dependency; a red 'BLOCKED' status chip appears next to a green checkmark labeled 'correctly stopped, not faked'

beats.role_note: ClaudeComposerAsk — REVISION; the real ODP→BigQuery pivot
beats.narration_text: Checking the actual data source before writing more code: USPTO's Open Data Portal has the claims text, but needs a government identity-verification step that takes real time. Google's Patents Public Data on BigQuery has the same claims text, confirmed via the actual table schema, no identity verification required. Switch the source. This is not undoing Week 3's work — it's recognizing a constraint that only became clear once the pipeline's real needs were understood.

props.command: claude "compare USPTO ODP vs Google Patents Public Data on BigQuery for claims text access — which has lower setup friction and a confirmed, current schema?"

beats.role_note: animated slot — confirmed schema, real field names
beats.narration_text: The schema, verified by hand, not trusted from documentation: claims_localized, with real text, language, and truncated fields — and citation, with publication_number and category. One dataset now serves both agents. Verifying it directly also caught something documentation wouldn't have shown: a publication-number format mismatch between older granted patents and newer applications, found by looking at five real sample rows instead of guessing twice.
beats.visual_intent: Manim: a table schema animates in field by field — claims_localized expanding to show text/language/truncated; citation expanding to show publication_number/category; a small red X then green check showing the format-mismatch catch

beats.narration_text: When to use this pattern: two independent readings of the same artifact, with a coordinator that names disagreement instead of quietly picking one. When not to: if the second reading would just repeat the first, skip the second agent — the complexity is only earned where the two views can actually conflict. And the smaller lesson underneath both agents: an honest NotImplementedError is worth more than code that looks done.
beats.visual_intent: Two overlapping circles — Claims Agent and Lineage Agent — with a small coordinator node between them labeled 'flags disagreement, doesn't resolve it'; text below: 'earned complexity, not default complexity'

beats.role_note: hai persona — CLI worked exercise, second-to-last beat, per skills/make/hai/SKILL.md Step 4
beats.narration_text: Here is what this looks like in a real session, on your own patent. Paste this in.

cli_exercise.ask: claude "Pull the claims_localized text for a patent (e.g. its publication number, formatted US-XXXXXXXX-A or -B) from patents-public-data.patents.publications on BigQuery, and summarize the independent claim's protection scope in plain terms."
cli_exercise.output_description: A short structured summary: what the independent claim covers, flagged as broad or narrow, with the raw claims text quoted below it for you to check against.
cli_exercise.change: Add: also pull the citation field and report whether backward citations are mostly the same assignee's own prior patents or a competitor's.
cli_exercise.output2_description: The same summary, now with a citation-character line — e.g. 'predominantly own prior work' — that tells you whether this filing looks like research continuity or competitive positioning.
cli_exercise.next_step: Run it on one real patent from a company you're actually researching, and check the claims text against the summary yourself before trusting either agent's reading.
